title: Teen Builds a Tongue-Controlled Wheelchair and Wins $10,000!
summary:
Have you ever tried to control a video game with just your tongue? That's kind of what Holly Tang, a 10th grader from California, invented — but for real life! She built a system called Tonguage that lets people control a wheelchair using their tongue and eye blinks. And she just won $10,000 for it!

Here's how it works: a normal laptop camera watches your face. When you move your tongue inside your mouth, it acts like a joystick. When you blink, that's like clicking a mouse. The system can tell the difference between the user and other people in the room, so it only follows the right person's commands. That's super important for safety.

Holly got the idea after visiting a rehabilitation center. She saw people who couldn't use their hands well and wanted to help them have more independence. She made sure her invention uses cheap, everyday cameras instead of expensive special equipment. "Mobility conditions don't discriminate," she said. "They can affect anyone of any income."

But Holly didn't stop at wheelchairs. She realized her system could also let people play video games! "We're so focused on giving people autonomy over basic tasks that we often leave out things like gaming," she said. "They deserve the freedom to play games and enjoy entertainment as well."

Holly won first place in the IEEE Presidents' Scholarship at a big science fair. Two other teens also won prizes: Partap Sidhu made a mind-controlled exoskeleton for legs, and Calvin Shang Hung built a robot that can handle rough terrain. All three are using their skills to help people with disabilities. Holly plans to study biomedical engineering in college. She says the most important part is empathy — understanding how your invention can change someone's life.
why_it_matters: A teenager close to your age used empathy and engineering to help people with disabilities, showing that young inventors can solve real problems.
